paragraphs: The Constitution proposed by the Convention may be considered from two general points of view. The FIRST concerns the sum or quantity of power that it vests in the government, including the restraints it imposes on the States. The SECOND concerns the particular structure of the government and the distribution of this power among its separate branches.

Under the FIRST view of the subject, two important questions arise. 1. Is any part of the powers transferred to the general government unnecessary or improper? 2. Is the entire mass of them dangerous to the portion of jurisdiction left in the individual States?
Is the aggregate power of the general government greater than ought to have been vested in it? This is the FIRST question.

Those who have attended with fairness to the arguments used against the extensive powers of the government cannot have missed that the authors of those arguments have given very little thought to how far these powers are necessary means of attaining a necessary end. They have preferred to dwell on the drawbacks that must unavoidably be mixed in with all political advantages, and on the possible abuses that must go along with every power or trust of which a beneficial use can be made. This way of handling the subject cannot impose on the good sense of the people of America. It may display the writer's subtlety; it may open a boundless field for rhetoric and declamation; it may inflame the passions of the unthinking and confirm the prejudices of the misthinking. But cool and fair-minded people will at once reflect that the purest of human blessings must have a portion of alloy in them; that the choice must always be of the GREATER good, not the PERFECT good, if not of the lesser evil; and that in every political institution a power to advance the public happiness involves a discretion that may be misapplied and abused. They will see, therefore, that in all cases where power is to be conferred, the point to be decided first is whether such a power is necessary to the public good. The next point, in case of an affirmative decision, is to guard as effectively as possible against a perversion of the power to the public detriment.

To form a correct judgment on this subject, it will be proper to review the several powers conferred on the government of the Union. To make this easier, they may be sorted into different classes according to the objects they relate to: 1. Security against foreign danger; 2. Regulation of the intercourse with foreign nations; 3. Maintenance of harmony and proper intercourse among the States; 4. Certain miscellaneous objects of general utility; 5. Restraint of the States from certain injurious acts; 6. Provisions for giving due effectiveness to all these powers.

The powers falling within the FIRST class are those of declaring war and granting letters of marque; of providing armies and fleets; of regulating and calling forth the militia; and of levying and borrowing money.

Security against foreign danger is one of the primary objects of civil society. It is an avowed and essential object of the American Union. The powers needed to attain it must be effectively entrusted to the federal councils.

Is the power of declaring war necessary? No one will answer this question in the negative, so it would be superfluous to enter into a proof of the affirmative. The existing Confederation establishes this power in the most ample form.
Is the power of raising armies and equipping fleets necessary? This is included in the preceding power. It is included in the power of self-defense.
But was it necessary to give an INDEFINITE POWER of raising TROOPS as well as providing fleets, and of maintaining both in PEACE as well as in WAR?

The answer to these questions has been anticipated too far in another place to allow an extensive discussion of them here. The answer indeed seems so obvious and conclusive that it scarcely justifies such a discussion anywhere. With what appearance of propriety could the force necessary for defense be limited by those who cannot limit the force of offense? If a federal Constitution could chain the ambition or set bounds to the exertions of all other nations, then indeed it might prudently chain the discretion of its own government and set bounds to the exertions for its own safety.

How could readiness for war in time of peace be safely prohibited, unless we could prohibit, in the same way, the preparations and establishments of every hostile nation? The means of security can only be regulated by the means and the danger of attack. In fact, they will always be determined by these rules and by no others. It is in vain to set up constitutional barriers against the impulse of self-preservation. It is worse than in vain, because it plants in the Constitution itself necessary usurpations of power, every precedent of which is a seed of unnecessary and multiplied repetitions. If one nation constantly maintains a disciplined army, ready for the service of ambition or revenge, it obliges the most peaceable nations within reach of its enterprises to take corresponding precautions. The fifteenth century was the unhappy period of military establishments in time of peace. They were introduced by Charles VII of France. All Europe has followed his example or been forced into it. Had other nations not followed it, all Europe would long ago have worn the chains of a universal monarch. If every nation except France were now to disband its peacetime establishments, the same result might follow. The veteran legions of Rome were more than a match for the undisciplined valor of all other nations and made her the mistress of the world.

It is no less true that the liberties of Rome proved the final victim of her military triumphs, and that the liberties of Europe, as far as they ever existed, have with few exceptions been the price of her military establishments. A standing force, therefore, is a dangerous provision, even though it may also be a necessary one. On the smallest scale it has its drawbacks. On an extensive scale its consequences may be fatal. On any scale it is an object of laudable caution and precaution. A wise nation will weigh all these considerations. It will not rashly shut itself off from any resource that may become essential to its safety, but it will use all its prudence to reduce both the necessity and the danger of resorting to one that may be ominous to its liberties.

The clearest marks of this prudence are stamped on the proposed Constitution. The Union itself, which it cements and secures, destroys every pretext for a military establishment that could be dangerous. America united, with a handful of troops or without a single soldier, presents a more forbidding posture to foreign ambition than America disunited, with a hundred thousand veterans ready for combat. It was remarked on a former occasion that the lack of this pretext saved the liberties of one nation in Europe. Because her island situation and her maritime resources made her impregnable to the armies of her neighbors, the rulers of Great Britain have never been able, by real or artificial dangers, to cheat the public into an extensive peacetime establishment. The distance of the United States from the powerful nations of the world gives them the same happy security. A dangerous establishment can never be necessary or plausible so long as they remain a united people. But let it never, for a moment, be forgotten that they owe this advantage to the Union alone. The moment of its dissolution will be the date of a new order of things. The fears of the weaker States, or the ambition of the stronger States or Confederacies, will set the same example in the New World that Charles VII set in the Old. The example will be followed here from the same motives that produced universal imitation there. Instead of drawing from our situation the precious advantage that Great Britain has drawn from hers, America will be only a copy of the continent of Europe. It will present liberty everywhere crushed between standing armies and perpetual taxes. The fortunes of disunited America will be even more disastrous than those of Europe. The sources of evil in Europe are confined to her own limits. No superior powers of another quarter of the globe intrigue among her rival nations, inflame their mutual animosities and make them the instruments of foreign ambition, jealousy and revenge. In America, the miseries springing from her internal jealousies, contentions and wars would be only a part of her lot. A plentiful addition of evils would have their source in the relation in which Europe stands to this quarter of the earth, and which no other quarter of the earth bears to Europe.

This picture of the consequences of disunion cannot be too highly colored or too often shown. Every man who loves peace, every man who loves his country, every man who loves liberty ought to keep it ever before his eyes, so that he may cherish in his heart a due attachment to the Union of America and be able to set a due value on the means of preserving it.

Next to the effective establishment of the Union, the best possible precaution against danger from standing armies is a limit on the term for which revenue may be appropriated to their support. The Constitution has prudently added this precaution. I will not repeat here the observations that, I flatter myself, have put this subject in a just and satisfactory light. But it may not be improper to take notice of an argument against this part of the Constitution that has been drawn from the policy and practice of Great Britain. It is said that keeping up an army in that kingdom requires an annual vote of the legislature, whereas the American Constitution has lengthened this critical period to two years. This is the form in which the comparison is usually put to the public. But is it a just form? Is it a fair comparison? Does the British Constitution restrain the discretion of Parliament to one year? Does the American Constitution impose on Congress appropriations for two years? On the contrary, the authors of the fallacy themselves cannot be unaware that the British Constitution fixes no limit whatever to the discretion of the legislature, and that the American Constitution ties the legislature down to two years as the longest permissible term.

Had the argument from the British example been stated truly, it would have run thus. The term for which supplies may be appropriated to the army establishment, though unlimited by the British Constitution, has nevertheless been limited in practice, by parliamentary discretion, to a single year. Now, in Great Britain the House of Commons is elected for seven years; so great a proportion of its members are elected by so small a proportion of the people; the electors are so corrupted by the representatives, and the representatives so corrupted by the Crown. If, in such a country, the representative body can possess a power to make appropriations to the army for an indefinite term, without desiring or without daring to extend the term beyond a single year, ought not suspicion herself to blush in pretending that the representatives of the United States cannot safely be trusted with discretion over such appropriations, expressly limited to the short period of TWO YEARS, when they are elected FREELY by the WHOLE BODY of the people every SECOND YEAR?

A bad cause seldom fails to betray itself. The management of the opposition to the federal government is an unvarying example of this truth. But among all the blunders that have been committed, none is more striking than the attempt to enlist on that side the prudent jealousy the people feel toward standing armies. The attempt has fully awakened public attention to that important subject. It has led to investigations that must end in a thorough and universal conviction of two things. The first is that the Constitution has provided the most effective guards against danger from that quarter. The second is that nothing short of a Constitution fully adequate to the national defense and the preservation of the Union can save America from as many standing armies as it may be split into States or Confederacies, and from such a progressive increase of these establishments in each as will make them as burdensome to the property and as ominous to the liberties of the people as any establishment that can become necessary under a united and effective government must be tolerable to the former and safe to the latter.

The obvious necessity of the power to provide and maintain a navy has protected that part of the Constitution from a spirit of censure that has spared few other parts. It must indeed be numbered among the greatest blessings of America that, as her Union will be the only source of her maritime strength, this strength will in turn be a principal source of her security against danger from abroad. In this respect our situation bears another likeness to the island advantage of Great Britain. The batteries best able to repel foreign attempts on our safety are happily such as can never be turned by a treacherous government against our liberties.

The inhabitants of the Atlantic frontier are all deeply interested in this provision for naval protection. They have hitherto been allowed to sleep quietly in their beds; their property has remained safe against the predatory spirit of lawless adventurers; their maritime towns have not yet been compelled to ransom themselves from the terrors of a conflagration by yielding to the exactions of daring and sudden invaders. These instances of good fortune are not to be ascribed to the capacity of the existing government to protect those from whom it claims allegiance, but to causes that are fleeting and deceptive. If we except perhaps Virginia and Maryland, which are peculiarly vulnerable on their eastern frontiers, no part of the Union ought to feel more anxiety on this subject than New York. Her seacoast is extensive. A very important district of the State is an island. The State itself is penetrated by a large navigable river for more than fifty leagues. The great emporium of its commerce, the great reservoir of its wealth, lies every moment at the mercy of events, and may almost be regarded as a hostage for shameful compliance with the dictates of a foreign enemy, or even with the rapacious demands of pirates and barbarians. Should war result from the precarious situation of European affairs, and all the unruly passions that attend it be let loose on the ocean, our escape from insults and depredations, not only on that element but in every part of the land bordering on it, will be truly miraculous. In the present condition of America, the States most immediately exposed to these calamities have nothing to hope from the phantom of a general government that now exists. And if their separate resources were equal to the task of fortifying themselves against the danger, the object to be protected would be almost consumed by the means of protecting it.
The power of regulating and calling forth the militia has already been sufficiently defended and explained.

The power of levying and borrowing money is the sinew of the power to be exerted in the national defense, and it is therefore properly placed in the same class. This power, too, has already been examined with much attention and has, I trust, been clearly shown to be necessary, both in the extent and in the form the Constitution gives it. I will add one further reflection only, addressed to those who contend that the power ought to have been restrained to external taxation, by which they mean taxes on articles imported from other countries. It cannot be doubted that this will always be a valuable source of revenue; that for a considerable time it must be a principal source; and that at this moment it is an essential one. But we may form very mistaken ideas on this subject if we do not keep in mind, in our calculations, that the amount of revenue drawn from foreign commerce must vary with the variations in both the quantity and the kind of imports, and that these variations do not correspond with the growth of population, which must be the general measure of the public wants. As long as agriculture continues to be the sole field of labor, the importation of manufactures must increase as the consumers multiply. As soon as domestic manufactures are begun by hands not needed for agriculture, the imported manufactures will decrease as the number of people increases. At a more remote stage, the imports may consist in considerable part of raw materials, which will be worked into articles for export and will therefore require the encouragement of bounties rather than to be loaded with discouraging duties. A system of government meant to last ought to contemplate these revolutions and be able to adapt itself to them.

Some who have not denied the necessity of the power of taxation have based a very fierce attack on the Constitution upon the language in which it is defined. It has been urged and echoed that the power "to lay and collect taxes, duties, imposts, and excises, to pay the debts, and provide for the common defense and general welfare of the United States," amounts to an unlimited commission to exercise every power that may be alleged to be necessary for the common defense or general welfare. No stronger proof could be given of how hard these writers are pressed for objections than their stooping to such a misconstruction.

Had no other enumeration or definition of the powers of Congress been found in the Constitution than the general expressions just cited, the authors of the objection might have had some color for it, though it would have been difficult to find a reason for so awkward a way of describing an authority to legislate in all possible cases. A power to destroy the freedom of the press or the trial by jury, or even to regulate the course of descents or the forms of conveyances, would be very singularly expressed by the words "to raise money for the general welfare."

But what color can the objection have when a specification of the objects alluded to by these general terms follows immediately, not even separated by a longer pause than a semicolon? If the different parts of the same instrument ought to be interpreted so as to give meaning to every part that will bear it, shall one part of the same sentence be excluded altogether from a share in the meaning? Shall the more doubtful and indefinite terms be kept in their full extent, and the clear and precise expressions be denied any meaning whatsoever? For what purpose could the enumeration of particular powers have been inserted, if these and all others were meant to be included in the preceding general power? Nothing is more natural or common than first to use a general phrase and then to explain and qualify it by a list of particulars. But the idea of an enumeration of particulars that neither explain nor qualify the general meaning, and can have no other effect than to confuse and mislead, is an absurdity. We are reduced to the dilemma of charging it either on the authors of the objection or on the authors of the Constitution, and we must take the liberty of supposing that it did not originate with the latter.

The objection is the more extraordinary because the language used by the Convention turns out to be a copy from the articles of Confederation. The objects of the Union among the States, as described in article third, are "their common defense, security of their liberties, and mutual and general welfare." The terms of article eighth are still more identical: "All charges of war and all other expenses that shall be incurred for the common defense or general welfare, and allowed by the United States in Congress, shall be defrayed out of a common treasury," etc. Similar language occurs again in article ninth. Interpret either of these articles by the rules that would justify the construction put on the new Constitution, and they vest in the existing Congress a power to legislate in all cases whatsoever. But what would have been thought of that assembly if, fastening on these general expressions and disregarding the specifications that determine and limit their meaning, it had exercised an unlimited power of providing for the common defense and general welfare? I appeal to the objectors themselves: would they in that case have used the same reasoning in justification of Congress as they now use against the Convention? How difficult it is for error to escape its own condemnation!
